claims.text: High-temperature structural stability of multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles is governed by compositional disorder, lattice strain, and surface energy.
High-temperature chemical stability of these nanoparticles is governed by compositional disorder, lattice strain, and surface energy.
The stability-governing interplay can be predicted using combined experiments, DFT, and MD simulations.
The stability-governing interplay can be optimized using combined experiments, DFT, and MD simulations.
Systematically varying composition, lattice structure, and surface modification will vary compositional disorder, lattice strain, and surface energy.
A balance among compositional disorder, lattice strain, and surface energy produces optimal nanoparticle stability.
Nanoparticles with optimized compositional disorder, lattice strain, and surface energy will show improved structural stability at 773–1923 K.
Nanoparticles with optimized compositional disorder, lattice strain, and surface energy will show improved chemical stability at 773–1923 K.
Improved structural and chemical stability will enhance catalytic performance.
Improved structural and chemical stability will enhance thermoelectric performance.
Nanoparticles with unoptimized compositional disorder, lattice strain, and surface energy will have lower high-temperature stability than optimized nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with unoptimized compositional disorder, lattice strain, and surface energy will have lower high-temperature performance than optimized nanoparticles.
The proposed relationship applies only within the explored compositions, lattice structures, surface modifications, and service regimes.
